payload.stem: In a mid-sized city, $240$ adults volunteer to participate in a study, and each chooses whether to follow the exercise plan or to not follow it. After the study period, the mean weight loss is higher in the group that used the exercise plan, and the difference is statistically significant. Which conclusion is justified by the design of this study?

options.text: The exercise plan caused the higher mean weight loss, but the result cannot be generalized beyond the adults in the study
options.why: Claims cause even though the participants chose their own group.

options.text: The exercise plan caused the higher mean weight loss, and the result can be generalized to all adults
options.why: Claims cause and generalization even though the participants were not randomly selected.

options.text: The result can be generalized to all adults, but it does not show that the exercise plan caused the higher mean weight loss
options.why: Refuses to conclude cause and generalizes even though the participants volunteered.

options.text: The result does not show that the exercise plan caused the higher mean weight loss and cannot be generalized to all adults
options.why: Without random assignment cause cannot be concluded, and without random selection the result cannot be generalized.

blueprint.concept: Decide which conclusions a study design justifies
student_thinking: Check whether treatments were assigned at random, which decides whether a cause-and-effect conclusion is justified
Check whether participants were randomly selected, which decides whether results can be generalized to the population

key_conditions.condition: random assignment allows a causal conclusion and random selection allows generalization
key_conditions.evidence: the stem states how participants were selected and how they were assigned to groups

misconceptions.description: refuses a conclusion that the design justifies

verification.independent_path: a truth table over the two design features is enumerated, exactly one of the four claims is allowed, and the sentences are generated from the same table

payload.explanation_en:
The correct answer is The result does not show that the exercise plan caused the higher mean weight loss and cannot be generalized to all adults. Without random assignment cause cannot be concluded, and without random selection the result cannot be generalized.
The exercise plan caused the higher mean weight loss, but the result cannot be generalized beyond the adults in the study is incorrect: Claims cause even though the participants chose their own group.
The exercise plan caused the higher mean weight loss, and the result can be generalized to all adults is incorrect: Claims cause and generalization even though the participants were not randomly selected.
The result can be generalized to all adults, but it does not show that the exercise plan caused the higher mean weight loss is incorrect: Refuses to conclude cause and generalizes even though the participants volunteered.

review.summary: The item is a clean standalone check of what the design justifies. Volunteers who chose their own groups mean no random selection and no random assignment, so neither causation nor generalization is justified. Option D is the unique key, and the independent solver agreed.

scope_skill.notes: The item targets topic 1.13 (experimental design) and skill 2.B. The dominant demand is deciding which conclusions a design justifies, using random assignment for cause and random selection for generalization.

key_scoring.notes: The stem states that adults volunteered and chose their own group. That removes both random selection and random assignment, so only option D is defensible. The other three options each make at least one unjustified claim.

stimulus_expression.notes: No stimulus is needed, and the stem is complete and clearly worded in US English. The options are parallel full sentences of similar length.

distractor_explanation.notes: Each wrong option encodes a distinct misconception: causation from self-selected groups, causation plus generalization from volunteers, and generalizing while denying causation. The explanation addresses each one. One small flaw is that the "why" for option C says it "refuses to conclude cause", which describes the sentence rather than a misconception. The option still reads as a plausible mistake, so this is minor.

payload.stem: The lengths of phone calls, in minutes, for calls to a help line are skewed to the right with mean $50$ and standard deviation $25$. The dotplot shown displays the means of $40$ simulated random samples of $100$ values from this population. Which describes the sampling distribution of the sample mean for samples of size $100$?

options.text: Skewed to the right like the population, with mean $50$ and standard deviation $2.5$
options.why: Believes the sampling distribution keeps the shape of the skewed population even with a large sample size.

options.text: Approximately normal, with mean $50$ and standard deviation $25$
options.why: Keeps the population standard deviation instead of dividing it by the square root of the sample size.

options.text: Approximately normal, with mean $50$ and standard deviation $0.25$
options.why: Divides the population standard deviation by $n$ instead of by the square root of $n$.

options.text: Approximately normal, with mean $50$ and standard deviation $2.5$
options.why: The mean of the sampling distribution is $\mu=50$ and its standard deviation is $\sigma/\sqrt{n}=25/\sqrt{100}=2.5$; with $100$ observations the Central Limit Theorem makes it approximately normal.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Describe the sampling distribution of a sample mean using the Central Limit Theorem
student_thinking: Find the mean and the standard deviation of the sampling distribution from the population values and the sample size
Decide the shape of the sampling distribution from the sample size even though the population is skewed

key_conditions.condition: the sampling distribution of the mean has mean mu, standard deviation sigma over root n and is approximately normal for large n
key_conditions.evidence: the sample size is large (at least 30) and the population standard deviation is given

verification.independent_path: 4000 simulated samples from a gamma population with the same mean and standard deviation reproduce the stated mean and standard deviation, and the plotted means are checked against them

payload.explanation_en:
The correct answer is Approximately normal, with mean $50$ and standard deviation $2.5$. The mean of the sampling distribution is $\mu=50$ and its standard deviation is $\sigma/\sqrt{n}=25/\sqrt{100}=2.5$; with $100$ observations the Central Limit Theorem makes it approximately normal.
Skewed to the right like the population, with mean $50$ and standard deviation $2.5$ is incorrect: Believes the sampling distribution keeps the shape of the skewed population even with a large sample size.
Approximately normal, with mean $50$ and standard deviation $25$ is incorrect: Keeps the population standard deviation instead of dividing it by the square root of the sample size.
Approximately normal, with mean $50$ and standard deviation $0.25$ is incorrect: Divides the population standard deviation by $n$ instead of by the square root of $n$.

scope_skill.notes: Directly targets the CLT and the mean and SD of the sampling distribution of the sample mean (topic 2.12). The description task fits skill 4.C well enough.

key_scoring.notes: The key is unique: approximately normal, mean 50, SD 2.5. The other three options each fail on shape or SD.

distractor_explanation.notes: The three distractors encode distinct misconceptions (keeps population shape, keeps sigma, divides by n). The explanation addresses each one.

payload.stem: A random sample of $336$ shoppers was classified by age group and by preferred payment method. A chi-square test of independence was carried out at the $\alpha=0.05$ significance level, and the conditions for inference were met. Computer output for the test is shown. Which conclusion is justified by the output?

stimulus.description: Computer output for a chi-square test of independence

output.title: Chi-Square Test of Independence: age group by preferred payment method

options.text: There is convincing evidence of an association between age group and preferred payment method only for the shoppers in the sample
options.why: Limits the conclusion to the sample even though the test is about the population.

options.text: There is convincing evidence that age group causes a difference in preferred payment method among all shoppers
options.why: Reads an association found by a test in an observational setting as cause and effect.

options.text: There is convincing evidence that age group and preferred payment method are independent among all shoppers
options.why: Reverses the conclusion: a small P-value is evidence against independence, not for it.

options.text: There is convincing evidence of an association between age group and preferred payment method among all shoppers
options.why: The P-value $0.0090$ is less than $0.05$, so the null hypothesis of independence is rejected and the conclusion is about the population.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Draw a conclusion from computer output for a chi-square test of independence
student_thinking: Compare the P-value in the output with the stated significance level to make a decision about the null hypothesis
State the conclusion in context about an association in the population without claiming cause or proving independence

key_conditions.condition: a P-value below alpha is evidence of an association in the population and a P-value above alpha is not
key_conditions.evidence: the output gives the statistic, degrees of freedom, P-value and the smallest expected count which shows the conditions hold

misconceptions.description: treats failing to reject as proof of independence
limits the conclusion to the sample

verification.independent_path: the chi-square statistic is recomputed from the expected counts, scipy.stats.chi2_contingency agrees and the tail area is also obtained by numerically integrating the chi-square density

payload.explanation_en:
The correct answer is There is convincing evidence of an association between age group and preferred payment method among all shoppers. The P-value $0.0090$ is less than $0.05$, so the null hypothesis of independence is rejected and the conclusion is about the population.
There is convincing evidence of an association between age group and preferred payment method only for the shoppers in the sample is incorrect: Limits the conclusion to the sample even though the test is about the population.
There is convincing evidence that age group causes a difference in preferred payment method among all shoppers is incorrect: Reads an association found by a test in an observational setting as cause and effect.
There is convincing evidence that age group and preferred payment method are independent among all shoppers is incorrect: Reverses the conclusion: a small P-value is evidence against independence, not for it.

review.summary: The item passes all five criteria. It is a clean, standard conclusion-from-output item on a chi-square test of independence. The P-value of 0.0090 is below alpha = 0.05, so the key is the only defensible choice: evidence of an association among all shoppers.

key_scoring.notes: The key (index 3) is unique. The sample is random, so the population-level conclusion is justified. The setting is observational, so the causal option is wrong. The smallest expected count of 23.27 is above 5, so the large-counts condition holds.

stimulus_expression.notes: The output includes the chi-square statistic, df, P-value and smallest expected count. The wording is clear.

payload.stem: A researcher compares reaction time, in milliseconds, for a new training method using independent random samples, and the conditions for inference are met. Computer output for a two-sample t procedure is shown, where $\mu_1$ is the mean for the New method group and $\mu_2$ is the mean for the Standard method group. At the $\alpha=0.05$ significance level, which conclusion is correct?

stimulus.description: Computer output for a two-sample t test and confidence interval

output.title: Two-Sample t Test and Confidence Interval

options.text: There is not convincing evidence that the population means differ, because the interval does not contain $0$
options.why: Draws the opposite conclusion from the interval: whether $0$ is inside the interval decides whether a difference of $0$ is plausible.

options.text: There is convincing evidence that the population means differ, because the interval does not contain $0$
options.why: The $95\%$ interval $(0.87, 9.33)$ does not contain $0$, which matches the P-value $0.0199$ being less than $0.05$ for a two-sided test.

options.text: There is convincing evidence that the population means differ, because the P-value is greater than $0.05$
options.why: Misstates how the P-value compares with the significance level when deciding the conclusion.

options.text: There is not convincing evidence that the population means differ, because the P-value is less than $0.05$
options.why: Reverses the meaning of the P-value: a small P-value is evidence against the null hypothesis, not for it.

student_thinking: Check whether the confidence interval for the difference contains zero and compare the two-sided P-value with the significance level
State a conclusion about the population means that is consistent with both and give the right reason

key_conditions.evidence: the output gives the interval, the P-value and the significance level is stated

misconceptions.description: draws the opposite conclusion from the interval
misstates the comparison of P with alpha
reverses the meaning of a small P-value

verification.independent_path: the Welch statistic, degrees of freedom, P-value (by numerical integration of the t density) and interval are recomputed from the summary statistics, and the interval and P-value must agree on the decision

payload.explanation_en:

There is not convincing evidence that the population means differ, because the interval does not contain $0$ is incorrect: Draws the opposite conclusion from the interval: whether $0$ is inside the interval decides whether a difference of $0$ is plausible.
There is convincing evidence that the population means differ, because the P-value is greater than $0.05$ is incorrect: Misstates how the P-value compares with the significance level when deciding the conclusion.
There is not convincing evidence that the population means differ, because the P-value is less than $0.05$ is incorrect: Reverses the meaning of the P-value: a small P-value is evidence against the null hypothesis, not for it.

payload.stem: A least-squares regression line is used to predict an exam score (in points) from the number of hours studied. The residual plot shown displays the residuals for the $24$ observations. Which statement is the most appropriate conclusion about the linear model?

stimulus.description: Residual plot with a horizontal line at zero

options.text: A linear model is appropriate because the residuals show no clear pattern
options.why: Overlooks the clear curved pattern in the residuals.

options.text: A linear model is appropriate because the residuals add up to $0$
options.why: Uses the fact that least-squares residuals always add up to $0$, which is true for every model and says nothing about fit.

options.text: A linear model is not appropriate because some of the residuals are far from $0$
options.why: Judges the model by how large individual residuals are rather than by the curved pattern they form.

options.text: A linear model is not appropriate because the residuals show a curved pattern
options.why: The residuals are positive at the ends and negative in the middle, a curved pattern that shows the linear model does not capture the relationship.

A linear model is not appropriate because some of the residuals are far from $0$ is incorrect: Judges the model by how large individual residuals are rather than by the curved pattern they form.

payload.stem: The scatterplot shown displays $11$ observations of the engine size (in liters) and the fuel efficiency (in miles per gallon).
